topics.title: ML lifecycle
topics.description: The lifecycle spans framing, data, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring rather than ending at model fit.

lessons.title: Follow the lifecycle
lessons.body: A machine-learning system moves through problem framing, data preparation, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. The work does not end when a model fits the training data: the deployed system must continue to serve its intended use.

lessons.title: Frame the problem and data
lessons.body: Define the decision the model will support, the outcome to predict, and how success will be measured. Gather data that represents the intended use and check its quality, permissions, and timing. For example, a demand forecast may use only information available before the forecast is made.

lessons.title: Train and evaluate
lessons.body: Train candidate models using the prepared training data, then evaluate them on data held out from fitting and model selection. Compare results with a baseline and check errors that matter to users. Record the data, code, and configuration so the result can be investigated or reproduced.

lessons.title: Deploy with safeguards
lessons.body: Deployment connects a model to the application or process that uses its predictions. Verify that serving inputs match the assumptions made during training, and define how to handle errors or unavailable predictions. A staged rollout and a documented rollback path can reduce the impact of a bad release.

lessons.title: Monitor and respond
lessons.body: After deployment, monitor service health and data changes, and evaluate prediction quality when outcome labels become available. An alert should lead to an investigation, not automatic retraining by default: a data pipeline error and a genuine change in user behavior require different responses. Feed what you learn back into the next iteration.

topics.title: Reproducible experiments
topics.description: Reproducibility requires recording data, code, configuration, environment, and relevant random seeds.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A reproducible experiment records enough information to rerun and investigate a result. Save the code revision, data version, training and evaluation settings, and relevant outputs. Without these records, a reported score is hard to compare or explain.

lessons.title: Identify the data
lessons.body: Record which data snapshot, split, and preprocessing steps were used. A dataset name alone is not enough if its records can change. Respect access and retention requirements: reproducibility does not mean keeping sensitive data indefinitely.

lessons.title: Record the environment
lessons.body: Capture relevant library versions, runtime, hardware, and configuration alongside the experiment. A dependency or hardware change can affect behavior even when the code is unchanged. Record the evaluation procedure and metric definitions as well as the final score.

lessons.title: Control randomness
lessons.body: Record seeds used for data splitting, initialization, and other random operations where applicable. A seed helps reproduce a run, but does not guarantee identical results across different hardware, library versions, or nondeterministic operations. Document any known sources of variation.

lessons.title: Verify with a rerun
lessons.body: Rerun an experiment from its recorded inputs and compare the resulting metrics and artifacts within an appropriate tolerance. If results differ, check the data, environment, and nondeterministic operations. Keep a clear record of the discrepancy rather than silently substituting a new result.

topics.title: Dataset versioning
topics.description: Dataset versions identify records and transformations used in an experiment, subject to privacy retention rules.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A dataset version identifies the data used for a particular experiment or model. A stable version lets a team distinguish one snapshot from another when records are added, corrected, or removed.

lessons.title: Record what changed
lessons.body: Track the source snapshot, selection rules, preprocessing code, and relevant schema alongside the version identifier. For example, a corrected delivery timestamp or a change to the lateness definition can alter both features and labels.

lessons.title: Connect data to runs
lessons.body: Record the dataset version and split with each experiment and model artifact. When an evaluation changes, this lineage helps determine whether the data, code, configuration, or another factor changed.

lessons.title: Protect access and retention
lessons.body: Versioning must follow privacy, access, and retention requirements. A deletion request may require removing or updating data in stored snapshots; reproducibility does not override those obligations. Document when an older version can no longer be reconstructed.

lessons.title: Verify a version
lessons.body: Check that the recorded identifier points to the intended snapshot and that preprocessing and split definitions are available. Compare expected schema and row counts, and investigate unexpected changes before using the version in training or evaluation.

topics.title: Model artifacts
topics.description: Artifacts include weights and metadata needed to interpret and serve a model safely.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A model artifact is a saved output of a training or packaging process. It may include learned weights, configuration, and metadata needed to load and identify the model. The exact files depend on the framework and deployment.

lessons.title: Include preprocessing
lessons.body: A model may depend on a fitted scaler, vocabulary, category mapping, or other preprocessing. Version these components with the model so serving uses compatible transformations. Saving weights alone may not reproduce the original predictions.

lessons.title: Record provenance
lessons.body: Link an artifact to its training run, data version, configuration, and evaluation results. Use immutable identifiers where possible. These records help a team investigate which model was trained and why it was selected.

lessons.title: Load safely
lessons.body: Restrict who can publish and access artifacts, verify their origin and integrity, and use supported loading formats. Some serialization formats can execute code when loaded, so do not load untrusted files blindly.

lessons.title: Prepare for deployment
lessons.body: Check the model and preprocessing versions together, test a representative prediction in the serving environment, and record the deployed version. Keep a compatible rollback artifact according to the team's retention and access policies.

topics.title: Training configuration
topics.description: Explicit configuration makes training choices reviewable and repeatable across environments.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Training configuration records choices such as data version, model settings, and optimization parameters. Making those choices explicit helps teams review and compare runs instead of relying on undocumented defaults.

lessons.title: Record key settings
lessons.body: Capture relevant parameters such as learning rate, batch size, epoch count, and model architecture. Record the data version, preprocessing, code version, and random seed when applicable. The important settings depend on the training workflow.

lessons.title: Validate configuration
lessons.body: Check required fields, types, and valid ranges before launching training. Reject a negative batch size or an unknown dataset version with a clear error rather than silently substituting a default.

lessons.title: Compare runs
lessons.body: Associate the resolved configuration with each run's metrics and artifacts. When comparing two experiments, identify which settings changed and whether the data split and evaluation procedure stayed the same.

lessons.title: Manage sensitive values
lessons.body: Keep credentials in an appropriate secret system rather than embedding them in configuration files or logs. Record the identity or reference needed for audit where policy permits, without exposing the secret value.

topics.title: Evaluation gates
topics.description: Gates prevent deployment when critical quality, compatibility, or safety criteria are unmet.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: An evaluation gate checks defined criteria before a candidate model can advance to deployment. It separates producing a model from deciding whether that model is suitable for the intended use.

lessons.title: Define criteria
lessons.body: A gate may include task quality, subgroup performance, latency, compatibility, or safety checks. Set thresholds and identify who owns them before evaluating candidates. Criteria should reflect the deployment context.

lessons.title: Use representative evidence
lessons.body: Evaluate with data and tests that reflect the intended use, while protecting a final test set from repeated tuning. Record dataset and model versions with the results. A single aggregate metric can hide important failures.

lessons.title: Handle failures
lessons.body: If a required check fails or cannot be evaluated, block promotion or follow an explicit exception process. Surface the reason to the responsible team. A missing result should not silently count as a pass.

lessons.title: Monitor after release
lessons.body: Passing a gate is evidence for a release decision, not a guarantee of future performance. Monitor production behavior and data changes, and keep a tested rollback path. Revisit criteria when the task or risks change.

topics.title: Model registry
topics.description: A registry tracks artifacts, metadata, approval, and deployment state across versions.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A model registry records model versions and related metadata so teams can track candidates and deployed artifacts. A registry supports governance, but its presence alone does not ensure a model is approved or safe.

lessons.title: Identify a version
lessons.body: Link each registered model version to its artifact and producing run. Record relevant data, preprocessing, and evaluation references. A mutable alias such as production can point to different versions over time.

lessons.title: Track review state
lessons.body: Record evaluation results and required approval decisions for a candidate. Define who may change its status and what evidence is needed. A version being registered is not the same as being authorized for deployment.

lessons.title: Connect deployment
lessons.body: Record which model and compatible preprocessing are deployed in each environment. Monitor alias changes and retain a way to identify the exact artifact used by a request or release where practical.

lessons.title: Manage access and lifecycle
lessons.body: Restrict who can publish, approve, or deploy versions, and define retention and retirement policies. Test that required rollback artifacts remain available. Registry metadata can be incomplete, so verify it against workflow records.

topics.title: CI for ML
topics.description: ML CI checks code, data contracts, reproducibility, and evaluation without requiring full retraining for every change.

lessons.title: What ML continuous integration checks
lessons.body: Continuous integration runs automated checks when a change is proposed. For machine learning, checks can cover application code, data contracts, training configuration, and model evaluation in addition to ordinary unit tests. The goal is to catch actionable problems early, not to assume every change needs a full production training run. Choose checks based on what changed and the risks involved.

lessons.title: Validate data contracts
lessons.body: A data contract describes expected properties such as field names, types, allowed values, and units. A CI check can detect a missing required column or an unexpected type using representative fixtures or a controlled sample. Passing a schema check does not prove the data is unbiased, fresh, or suitable for training. Treat those as separate questions.

lessons.title: Run small reproducible checks
lessons.body: A small fixture and a short training or inference smoke test can reveal broken code paths without the expense of full retraining. Record relevant dependencies, configuration, and random seeds where feasible, while recognizing that some operations may remain nondeterministic. A smoke test checks that a path runs; it does not establish production model quality. Make failures visible and reproducible.

lessons.title: Test model behavior
lessons.body: A model evaluation suite can check a fixed set of representative cases and relevant metrics against agreed thresholds. Include important slices and error types where the sample is adequate. Separate fast checks in CI from larger, scheduled or release-stage evaluations when necessary. Avoid repeatedly tuning against a supposedly final test set.

lessons.title: Make failures actionable
lessons.body: A useful pipeline reports which check failed, the relevant version, and enough context to reproduce the issue without exposing sensitive data. Decide which failures block a merge or release and who owns investigation. Track flaky or nondeterministic checks instead of silently ignoring them. Version the evaluation inputs and thresholds so changes to the check are reviewable.

topics.title: CD for models
topics.description: Model delivery automates controlled promotion while preserving approvals, canaries, and rollback.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Model delivery automates controlled promotion while preserving approvals, canaries, and rollback. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Stage a release
lessons.body: A delivery pipeline should promote an evaluated artifact through explicit stages, not train a fresh model during deployment. Keep the candidate identifier and evaluation report attached to each approval so reviewers can tell exactly what will receive traffic.

lessons.title: Limit exposure and recover
lessons.body: Route a small, measurable share of requests to a candidate while tracking predefined service and quality guardrails. If a guardrail fails, restore the prior known-good version and confirm traffic has actually moved back.

topics.title: Batch and online serving
topics.description: Serving mode determines schedule, latency, scaling, and freshness needs.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Serving mode determines schedule, latency, scaling, and freshness needs. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Choose by response need
lessons.body: Batch inference processes a defined set of records on a schedule, making it efficient when a result can wait. Online inference serves a request immediately and is appropriate when a user or system needs a low-latency answer.

lessons.title: Plan freshness and capacity
lessons.body: A daily batch may be economical but leave decisions based on yesterday's data; an online endpoint can be fresh but needs capacity for traffic spikes. Choose the mode against the required freshness, latency, cost, and recovery constraints.

topics.title: Monitoring basics
topics.description: Monitoring covers service health and prediction behavior, though quality labels may arrive late.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Monitoring covers service health and prediction behavior, though quality labels may arrive late. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Separate service and model signals
lessons.body: Request failures and latency describe whether the serving system is healthy; input distributions and later outcome metrics describe model behavior. Track both because a fast, available endpoint can still make poor predictions.

lessons.title: Act on delayed evidence
lessons.body: When labels arrive weeks later, use immediate operational signals to detect outages and data checks to catch malformed inputs, but do not claim those proxies prove predictive quality. Reconcile eventual labels against the model's recorded predictions.

topics.title: Data quality checks
topics.description: Checks detect schema changes, missing values, invalid ranges, and distribution anomalies.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Checks detect schema changes, missing values, invalid ranges, and distribution anomalies. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Validate before training
lessons.body: Check required columns, types, missingness, allowed ranges, and row volumes before a dataset enters training. A failed schema check should stop or quarantine the run rather than silently coercing unexpected values.

lessons.title: Set meaningful bounds
lessons.body: A rule should distinguish harmless variation from a broken feed: compare counts with expected ranges and validate domain constraints such as nonnegative amounts. Review alerts against source changes before loosening a threshold.

topics.title: Model drift
topics.description: Drift signals changing inputs or relationships but does not alone prove declining outcome quality.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Drift signals changing inputs or relationships but does not alone prove declining outcome quality. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Recognize a drift signal
lessons.body: Drift means the observed input or prediction distribution has changed relative to a reference period. A change can come from seasonality or a population shift, so it is evidence to investigate rather than proof that accuracy fell.

lessons.title: Connect inputs to outcomes
lessons.body: Compare drifted features with delayed labels, segment metrics, and known product changes to determine whether model quality or only the population changed. Escalate according to impact and retrain only after a validated candidate improves the relevant outcomes.

topics.title: Incident response
topics.description: Incidents need defined severity, owners, rollback, communication, and post-incident learning.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Incidents need defined severity, owners, rollback, communication, and post-incident learning. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Triage with ownership
lessons.body: An incident process states how to classify impact, who is on call, and where to find the current production model and runbook. Assign an owner and preserve key timestamps and evidence as soon as the issue is identified.

lessons.title: Recover and learn
lessons.body: Use a tested rollback or mitigation when user impact warrants it, then verify service and prediction behavior after the change. Record the cause and follow-up actions so the same failure is less likely to recur.

topics.title: Retraining decisions
topics.description: Retraining should respond to evidence and validation rather than schedule alone.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Retraining should respond to evidence and validation rather than schedule alone. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Use evidence to trigger training
lessons.body: A fixed calendar can create unnecessary runs or miss a sudden change. Combine drift or data-quality alerts with outcome evidence and operational context to decide whether retraining is justified.

lessons.title: Validate before replacing
lessons.body: A newly trained model is only a candidate: compare it with the current version on a representative, held-out evaluation and required slices. Promote it only when quality, safety, and deployment checks pass; otherwise keep the current model.

topics.title: Experiment tracking
topics.description: Tracking records parameters, metrics, and artifact references so results can be compared.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Experiment tracking records the inputs and results of model runs so a team can compare and investigate them. A run can include parameters, metric definitions, dataset and code versions, and references to model artifacts.

lessons.title: Identify the run
lessons.body: Give each run a distinct identifier and record its data snapshot, split, code revision, environment, and configuration. Store the preprocessing and evaluation settings as well as the training settings so another person can understand the reported result.

lessons.title: Compare fairly
lessons.body: Compare candidates using the same validation split and metric definitions when possible. A higher score on a different dataset or with a different threshold is not necessarily an improvement. Keep a final test set separate from repeated model selection.

lessons.title: Link artifacts
lessons.body: Associate the trained model, preprocessing artifacts, and evaluation reports with the run that produced them. References should identify the exact versions and respect access controls. A metric without the corresponding model and data lineage is difficult to audit.

lessons.title: Investigate variation
lessons.body: Record relevant seeds and environment details, then compare repeated runs when randomness matters. A seed alone cannot guarantee identical results across nondeterministic operations or different environments. Document discrepancies and preserve only data permitted by retention policies.

topics.title: Feature pipelines
topics.description: Pipelines define transformations consistently for training and serving.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A feature pipeline turns raw data into model inputs through a defined sequence of transformations. The same feature meaning must be preserved when preparing training examples and serving predictions.

lessons.title: Fit only on training data
lessons.body: Some transformations learn parameters from data, such as a scaler's mean or a vocabulary. Fit those parameters on the training partition, then apply the fitted transformation to validation, test, and serving data. Fitting on held-out data can leak information.

lessons.title: Preserve the transformation
lessons.body: Save the fitted preprocessing artifact and its version with the model. For example, the same category mapping used during training should encode serving inputs. Define how to handle unknown categories and missing values.

lessons.title: Respect prediction time
lessons.body: Construct historical features using information available when each prediction would have been made. A transaction recorded or published later should not enter an earlier example merely because it appears in the current database.

lessons.title: Test both paths
lessons.body: Run representative raw inputs through offline and online paths and compare feature values, types, units, and missing-value behavior. Include edge cases and monitor feature freshness after release. Parity on tested inputs does not by itself prove the model is accurate.

topics.title: Data contracts
topics.description: Contracts specify expected schemas and value constraints at pipeline boundaries.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A data contract describes expectations at a boundary between a data producer and consumer. It can cover schema, value constraints, freshness, and how incompatible changes are handled.

lessons.title: Specify a schema
lessons.body: Name required fields, their types, and whether values may be missing. For example, an event may require an event ID and a timestamp. Schema validity alone does not establish that the event is accurate or appropriate for a model.

lessons.title: Specify value and timing rules
lessons.body: Define constraints such as valid ranges, allowed categories, units, and expected arrival times. A numeric temperature in the wrong unit can pass a type check but violate the intended meaning. State which team owns the rule and what happens when it fails.

lessons.title: Manage changes
lessons.body: Version contract changes and communicate them to consumers before rollout. Adding an optional field may be compatible for one consumer but not another, so check the actual readers and policies. Breaking changes need a coordinated migration.

lessons.title: Enforce and monitor
lessons.body: Validate data at the agreed boundary and surface failures through the pipeline's normal error and alerting process. Test both valid and invalid examples, monitor freshness and quality, and investigate violations. Avoid silently treating rejected data as successful input.

topics.title: Workflow orchestration
topics.description: Orchestrators coordinate dependent tasks with retries and recorded status.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Workflow orchestration coordinates tasks such as data validation, training, and evaluation. An orchestrator tracks dependencies and run status so a downstream task can wait for its required inputs.

lessons.title: Define dependencies
lessons.body: A training task may depend on a successful data validation task, and evaluation may depend on the trained model. Represent these dependencies explicitly rather than relying on task start times alone.

lessons.title: Handle failures and retries
lessons.body: A transient failure may be retryable, but repeated operations must handle side effects safely. Define retry limits and distinguish failures that need investigation. Do not mark a failed validation task as successful merely to keep the pipeline moving.

lessons.title: Record run state
lessons.body: Track task status, inputs, outputs, timestamps, and relevant versions. These records help diagnose failures and determine whether an upstream result can be reused. Avoid logging secrets or unnecessary sensitive data.

lessons.title: Test recovery
lessons.body: Exercise failure, retry, and restart scenarios before relying on automation. Verify that only valid dependencies run and that outputs are not duplicated by unsafe retries. Monitor the workflow after deployment.

topics.title: Artifact storage
topics.description: Artifact stores retain versioned models and related files with access and lifecycle policies.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: An artifact store retains files produced by a workflow, such as a model, preprocessing package, or evaluation report. Versioned artifacts support traceability and controlled deployment.

lessons.title: Record artifact identity
lessons.body: Assign a stable version or immutable identifier and link the artifact to its producing run. Record relevant dependencies and metadata. A mutable filename alone may refer to different contents over time.

lessons.title: Protect access
lessons.body: Grant read and write permissions according to each role's needs, and protect artifacts in transit and at rest according to policy. Restrict who can publish or replace release artifacts; not every reader should be a writer.

lessons.title: Manage the lifecycle
lessons.body: Define retention, deletion, and archival rules for model files and related reports. Keep required rollback versions available while honoring privacy and legal requirements. Account for copies and dependent releases.

lessons.title: Verify before use
lessons.body: Check that the requested version and compatible dependencies are available before deployment. Verify integrity against a trusted expected digest or signature where supported. Test retrieval and recovery rather than assuming stored artifacts will always be usable.

topics.title: Containerized training
topics.description: Containers package dependencies and runtime assumptions for consistent execution.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A training container packages an application and its runtime dependencies into an image. It can make environments more consistent, but it does not by itself identify data, hardware, or every source of randomness.

lessons.title: Build an image
lessons.body: Specify a base image, application code, and required dependencies using the project's supported build process. Pin or otherwise record versions and identify the resulting image by an immutable digest where possible.

lessons.title: Provide runtime inputs
lessons.body: Pass configuration and data references through controlled interfaces. Supply secrets through an appropriate secret system rather than baking them into an image or logging them. Record the resolved nonsecret settings for the run.

lessons.title: Run with required resources
lessons.body: The host and container runtime must provide compatible hardware, drivers, and resource limits. A container image that works on one machine may behave differently if those requirements are missing elsewhere.

lessons.title: Verify the artifact
lessons.body: Test the image with representative inputs and record its digest, code, data version, and outputs. Scan and update dependencies according to policy. A container improves packaging consistency but does not guarantee bit-for-bit reproducibility.

topics.title: Registry stages
topics.description: Stages communicate readiness and approval but should reflect evidence rather than labels alone.

lessons.title: Record model versions
lessons.body: A model registry records model artifacts and their versions alongside metadata needed to identify and manage them. A stage or status can communicate where a version is in an organization's release process. The exact stages depend on the registry and team workflow. A label helps coordination but does not itself prove a model is safe or ready.

lessons.title: Define promotion criteria
lessons.body: Before moving a candidate to a production-ready state, define the required evidence: for example, evaluation results, compatibility checks, and an authorized approval. Record who made the decision and which artifact was reviewed. A passing metric on one dataset may not satisfy every requirement. Promotion criteria should match the application's risk and intended use.

lessons.title: Deploy the intended artifact
lessons.body: The artifact deployed to serving should be the one that was evaluated and approved, along with compatible preprocessing and dependencies. A registry label that points to a different version can otherwise make the deployment misleading. Verify the resolved version and artifact identity at deployment time. Record the deployment so operators can trace a prediction back to its release.

lessons.title: Plan rollback
lessons.body: A rollback should restore a known compatible release, not merely an old model file. Check whether feature definitions, preprocessing, dependencies, and serving configuration match that release. Keep a documented process for choosing and deploying the previous approved version. Verify the rollback and continue monitoring after it completes.

lessons.title: Control and audit changes
lessons.body: Limit who can register, approve, relabel, or deploy models according to the organization's access rules. Keep an audit trail of changes to versions, evidence, and release decisions. Periodically review whether a registry status still reflects the current model, data, and evaluation context. A stale approval may not cover a changed environment.

topics.title: Deployment strategies
topics.description: Canary and blue-green releases limit exposure and simplify rollback.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Canary and blue-green releases limit exposure and simplify rollback. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Compare canary and blue-green
lessons.body: A canary sends a small fraction of live traffic to a candidate while the existing version continues to serve most requests. Blue-green keeps two environments available and switches traffic between them, enabling a quick switch back if compatibility and capacity are ready.

lessons.title: Define a guarded rollout
lessons.body: Choose the rollout method based on traffic shape, state compatibility, and the ability to observe outcomes. Set explicit error, latency, and quality thresholds before increasing exposure; do not treat a successful process start as evidence of a safe release.

topics.title: Prediction logging
topics.description: Logs enable diagnosis and audit but require minimization, access controls, and retention limits.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Logs enable diagnosis and audit but require minimization, access controls, and retention limits. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Log for traceability
lessons.body: A prediction record can link a request identifier, model version, timestamp, and carefully selected input or output fields to later outcomes. That linkage helps diagnose regressions, but logging every raw feature is neither necessary nor safe by default.

lessons.title: Minimize and protect records
lessons.body: Exclude direct identifiers and sensitive fields unless there is a documented need, restrict access, and apply retention limits. Test that logs still support the intended investigation after minimization and that deletion policies cover copies and exports.

topics.title: Service health monitoring
topics.description: Availability, errors, latency, and saturation reveal serving problems before labels arrive.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Availability, errors, latency, and saturation reveal serving problems before labels arrive. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Read the four signals
lessons.body: Availability, error rate, latency, and resource saturation describe distinct failure modes. A service can meet its availability target while latency or saturation steadily worsens, so inspect the signals together.

lessons.title: Connect symptoms to action
lessons.body: A rising timeout rate alongside a full worker pool suggests a capacity or dependency problem, while an isolated model-quality shift calls for a different investigation. Page the responsible owner using thresholds tied to user impact, not every noisy fluctuation.

topics.title: Data drift monitoring
topics.description: Distribution changes are investigation signals, not proof of model quality degradation.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Distribution changes are investigation signals, not proof of model quality degradation. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Choose a reference carefully
lessons.body: Drift monitoring compares recent feature values with a documented baseline that represents an appropriate operating period. If the baseline includes a known outage or excludes normal seasonality, alerts can mislead.

lessons.title: Investigate before reacting
lessons.body: Check which features moved, whether collection or product behavior changed, and whether affected records are valid. Use labeled outcomes when available before concluding that a drift alert requires retraining or rollback.

topics.title: Label delay
topics.description: Delayed outcomes require distinguishing immediate proxies from confirmed predictive quality.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Delayed outcomes require distinguishing immediate proxies from confirmed predictive quality. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Distinguish proxy from outcome
lessons.body: Latency, prediction volume, and schema validity are available quickly, but they do not directly establish whether a prediction was correct. A delayed business outcome or adjudicated label is stronger evidence of predictive quality.

lessons.title: Align predictions and labels
lessons.body: Store a stable prediction identifier and the model version so a label arriving later can be joined to the original decision. Track label completeness and delay by cohort to avoid comparing mature and incomplete evaluation windows.

topics.title: Rollback readiness
topics.description: Rollback requires a known-good artifact, compatible interface, and tested procedure.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Rollback requires a known-good artifact, compatible interface, and tested procedure. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Keep a known-good release
lessons.body: Rollback needs the previous approved model artifact, its preprocessing and serving configuration, and a compatible interface. A model file alone may not recreate the behavior that served production.

lessons.title: Test the recovery path
lessons.body: Practice switching traffic to the prior version and checking health, feature compatibility, and downstream effects. Record who can initiate rollback and how to avoid overwriting the evidence needed to diagnose the failed release.

topics.title: Access control
topics.description: Least privilege protects datasets, registries, secrets, and production endpoints.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Least privilege protects datasets, registries, secrets, and production endpoints. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Apply least privilege
lessons.body: Give each training job, reviewer, and serving service only the data and actions it needs. A read-only analyst should not be able to replace a production registry alias or retrieve deployment secrets.

lessons.title: Separate identities and credentials
lessons.body: Use managed identities or scoped short-lived credentials for automated jobs rather than embedding secrets in notebooks, images, or logs. Review access periodically and revoke credentials when a workload or owner changes.

topics.title: Runbooks and ownership
topics.description: Runbooks and named owners make model behavior and incident steps discoverable.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Runbooks and named owners make model behavior and incident steps discoverable. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Make ownership actionable
lessons.body: A runbook should identify the service owner, alert meaning, first diagnostic checks, and escalation route. An unowned alert or generic instruction to "check the model" leaves responders without a safe next step.

lessons.title: Keep operational guidance current
lessons.body: Link the runbook to the deployed model and dependency versions, then update it after changes and incidents. Rehearse a realistic failure so the team can verify that the steps and contacts work under pressure.

topics.title: Feature parity
topics.description: Parity tests verify transformations match between offline training and online serving paths.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Feature parity means the offline and online paths apply equivalent feature definitions for the same entity and point in time. A mismatch can occur even when the model artifact itself is unchanged, making offline evaluation unrepresentative of serving behavior.

lessons.title: Compare the same inputs
lessons.body: Construct test cases with identical raw values, timestamps, and expected availability for both paths. Compare resulting feature names, types, units, missing-value handling, and values within justified numeric tolerances. A different point-in-time join can produce a mismatch even if individual transformations look identical.

lessons.title: Check time and freshness
lessons.body: Offline training must use only data available at the historical prediction time. Online serving must respect publication delays, time zones, and freshness requirements. For example, a daily aggregate published after a decision should not be included in the offline feature for that decision.

lessons.title: Investigate mismatches
lessons.body: A mismatch may come from code versions, defaults, category mappings, source updates, or serialization. Log enough lineage to trace the raw input and transformation version without exposing unnecessary sensitive data. Fix the source of the difference and rerun the parity cases.

lessons.title: Guard the release
lessons.body: Run parity tests as part of feature or model changes and include boundary cases such as missing fields and late-arriving data. Monitor production feature distributions and freshness after deployment. Passing parity tests only covers the tested cases; it does not prove the model is accurate.

topics.title: Workflow DAGs
topics.description: DAGs encode dependencies and support selective retries without repeating unrelated work.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, represents workflow tasks and their dependencies without cycles. A training workflow might validate data, train a model, evaluate it, and then conditionally publish an artifact.

lessons.title: Define dependencies
lessons.body: A task can start only when its required upstream conditions are satisfied. If evaluation depends on a trained model, its dependency must point from training to evaluation. Independent validation tasks can run in parallel when their inputs and resource limits permit.

lessons.title: Design retries
lessons.body: A failed task can often be retried without rerunning unrelated completed tasks, but this depends on the workflow engine and artifact validity. Make side effects idempotent or otherwise protect them against duplicate execution. Distinguish transient failures from invalid inputs that need correction.

lessons.title: Track artifacts and versions
lessons.body: Record which data snapshot, code version, configuration, and upstream artifacts each task used. A retry or cache reuse is only valid when its inputs and relevant dependencies match. Avoid overwriting a shared output with an ambiguous version.

lessons.title: Observe and recover
lessons.body: Monitor task status, duration, retries, and dependency failures. Alert owners when a workflow stalls and define how to resume or rerun it safely. A completed DAG indicates its tasks ran according to their checks; it does not by itself prove the resulting model is suitable for deployment.

topics.title: Immutable snapshots
topics.description: Snapshots prevent mutable source tables from silently changing experiment meaning.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: An immutable snapshot identifies a fixed version of data used for an experiment or pipeline run. It prevents later edits to a mutable source from silently changing what that recorded run refers to.

lessons.title: Identify the snapshot
lessons.body: Record an immutable version or snapshot identifier with the run, along with relevant source and preprocessing information. A timestamp alone may not identify an exact dataset if records can be corrected or backfilled later.

lessons.title: Preserve the transformation
lessons.body: Data identity also depends on the query, code, configuration, and feature transformations used to construct the training set. Capture these alongside the snapshot so another run can understand how inputs were produced.

lessons.title: Verify and control access
lessons.body: Check that the selected version is accessible and matches expected schema and quality constraints. Restrict access according to data policy and account for retention or deletion requirements. An immutable reference does not eliminate privacy obligations.

lessons.title: Reproduce and compare
lessons.body: Use the recorded snapshot and pipeline versions to reproduce or investigate a result where possible. Record environment and randomness as needed, and compare artifacts and metrics. Reusing the same snapshot alone does not guarantee bit-for-bit reproducibility.

topics.title: Lineage and provenance
topics.description: Lineage links data, code, features, artifacts, and deployment for audit and debugging.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Lineage records relationships among inputs, transformations, model artifacts, and deployments. Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced. Together they support investigation and audit.

lessons.title: Trace training inputs
lessons.body: Connect a training run to data snapshots, feature definitions, preprocessing, code, and configuration. Use stable version identifiers where available. A mutable dataset name alone does not identify the exact input.

lessons.title: Trace outputs to deployment
lessons.body: Record which run produced a model artifact and which deployment uses it, including compatible preprocessing. This link helps identify affected deployments when a data or code issue is discovered.

lessons.title: Investigate an incident
lessons.body: Starting from a production model, follow its recorded dependencies to identify the relevant data and transformations. Confirm the records against artifacts and logs. A missing lineage edge is a gap to investigate, not proof that no dependency exists.

lessons.title: Maintain trustworthy records
lessons.body: Capture lineage as part of the workflow, restrict unauthorized changes, and test that records are complete enough for the intended investigation. Apply retention and privacy policies; lineage supports reproducibility but does not guarantee it.

topics.title: Automated validation
topics.description: Validation checks schema, quality, safety, and compatibility before a candidate advances.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Automated validation runs defined checks on data, artifacts, and model behavior before a workflow advances. It can detect known problems consistently, but the checks must match the intended deployment.

lessons.title: Validate inputs
lessons.body: Check required fields, types, ranges, freshness, and other data contracts before training or inference. A schema-valid dataset may still contain incorrect or unrepresentative values, so include appropriate quality checks.

lessons.title: Validate the candidate
lessons.body: Evaluate task metrics, important subgroup behavior where feasible, and compatibility with serving components. Include safety checks relevant to the task. Record the model and dataset versions used for each result.

lessons.title: Handle failures
lessons.body: Block advancement or follow a defined exception process when a required check fails or cannot run. Surface the reason and preserve useful evidence for investigation. Missing results must not silently count as passing.

lessons.title: Maintain checks
lessons.body: Test the checks with both valid and intentionally invalid examples. Monitor false alarms and missed issues, update rules as data or requirements change, and review results after deployment. Passing automation is not proof of complete safety.

topics.title: Canary analysis
topics.description: Canary analysis compares candidate and control under traffic with predefined rollback conditions.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A canary release sends a limited portion of traffic to a candidate while a control continues serving comparable traffic. Teams compare defined metrics before deciding whether to expand, hold, or roll back.

lessons.title: Define the comparison
lessons.body: Choose control and candidate versions, traffic allocation, metrics, and observation windows before rollout. Ensure assignment is appropriate for the service and that both versions receive comparable traffic where possible.

lessons.title: Set decision rules
lessons.body: Define thresholds for errors, latency, and task quality as well as conditions that require investigation or rollback. Some outcome labels arrive later than operational metrics, so a short canary may not reveal all quality problems.

lessons.title: Interpret evidence
lessons.body: Small traffic samples produce uncertain estimates. Inspect traffic mix and relevant groups, and account for monitoring delays. A passing short test is evidence for a decision, not a guarantee of long-term safety.

lessons.title: Recover safely
lessons.body: Keep a tested path to restore a compatible control release, including preprocessing and dependencies. Monitor the candidate and control throughout the rollout, record the decision, and investigate unexpected behavior before expanding traffic.

topics.title: Shadow evaluation
topics.description: Shadow deployment exercises a candidate without serving its decisions to users.

lessons.title: Run a candidate in shadow
lessons.body: In shadow evaluation, a candidate model receives inputs alongside the serving model, but its decisions are not used to control the user-facing result. This lets a team examine candidate behavior under realistic traffic before promotion. It does not by itself establish that the candidate is safe or ready. The shadow path must not cause unintended side effects.

lessons.title: Keep the comparison fair
lessons.body: Compare models on the same eligible inputs and record their versions, preprocessing, and execution conditions. Check whether both paths receive the same information at the same time and whether sampling excludes important cases. A mismatch in feature freshness can look like a model difference. Measure and document any differences that cannot be eliminated.

lessons.title: Prevent side effects
lessons.body: A shadow path must not send duplicate emails, execute purchases, or write decisions to live systems. Disable or isolate downstream actions and verify that logs or metrics do not leak protected inputs. If the candidate invokes tools, use safe substitutes or controls designed for the evaluation. A label saying shadow is not enough to prevent effects.

lessons.title: Evaluate delayed outcomes
lessons.body: Some outcomes, such as whether a transaction was fraudulent, are known only later. Store authorized identifiers needed to join predictions to outcomes, and report which labels are still pending. A candidate may have different scores from the serving model without being better or worse. Compare task metrics once enough relevant outcomes are available.

lessons.title: Decide whether to promote
lessons.body: Define evaluation windows, quality measures, operational limits, and decision criteria before reviewing results. Consider sampling uncertainty, relevant groups, latency, cost, and policy requirements. Shadow traffic does not fully reproduce the feedback or effects of actually serving the candidate. A controlled rollout may still be needed after shadow evaluation.

topics.title: Drift response
topics.description: Drift and delayed-label signals require investigation and defined actions rather than automatic retraining.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Drift and delayed-label signals require investigation and defined actions rather than automatic retraining. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Triage the changed population
lessons.body: Break a drift alert down by feature, segment, source, and time window; verify whether the change is a collection defect, expected seasonality, or a genuine population shift. This narrows the cause before a model change is considered.

lessons.title: Choose an evidence-based response
lessons.body: When labels are delayed, maintain existing guardrails and gather outcome evidence rather than automatically retraining on recent unlabeled data. If a material, harmful regression is confirmed, follow the approved mitigation or rollback policy and record the decision.

topics.title: Retraining pipelines
topics.description: Retraining needs controlled data windows, validation, approvals, and artifact lineage.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Retraining needs controlled data windows, validation, approvals, and artifact lineage. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Make training inputs explicit
lessons.body: Pin a time-bounded dataset snapshot, feature definitions, code revision, and configuration for every run. Explicit inputs prevent a retry from silently consuming a newer data window than the original attempt.

lessons.title: Gate and publish candidates
lessons.body: Run data validation and representative evaluation before producing a versioned candidate artifact; then record lineage and route it through review. A scheduled pipeline can create candidates, but it should not bypass promotion policy or replace production merely because a run succeeded.

topics.title: Promotion policy
topics.description: Promotion maps evidence and approvals to a production state, preventing unreviewed deployment.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Promotion maps evidence and approvals to a production state, preventing unreviewed deployment. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Translate evidence into policy
lessons.body: A promotion policy names required evaluation suites, slice thresholds, approvals, and compatibility checks for each transition. A single aggregate metric or a green training job is not enough if a required subgroup or serving contract fails.

lessons.title: Make transitions auditable
lessons.body: Record the candidate version, evidence, approver, decision, and time when a model moves stages. If any gate is missing or stale, keep the model in its current stage and request the missing evidence rather than inferring approval.

topics.title: Serving autoscaling
topics.description: Autoscaling must account for model load, warmup, concurrency, and accelerator capacity.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Autoscaling must account for model load, warmup, concurrency, and accelerator capacity. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Measure model-specific capacity
lessons.body: Estimate throughput and latency under representative batch sizes, concurrency, model load time, and accelerator memory use. CPU-based scaling alone may miss GPU saturation or repeated model warmups.

lessons.title: Prevent scale oscillation
lessons.body: Set minimum warm capacity and meaningful scale-up and scale-down windows based on traffic bursts and model startup time. Validate that the cluster has quota and that scaling does not exceed safe accelerator capacity or starve other workloads.

topics.title: Model SLOs
topics.description: SLOs cover inference latency, availability, freshness, and where possible task quality.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: SLOs cover inference latency, availability, freshness, and where possible task quality. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Specify measurable objectives
lessons.body: Define service-level objectives for latency percentiles, successful requests, and feature freshness, with a window and eligible traffic population. Predictive quality can be included only where trustworthy labels or reviewed evaluation data exist.

lessons.title: Use error budgets deliberately
lessons.body: An error budget connects observed SLO misses to release risk: when the budget is exhausted, pause risky changes and prioritize reliability work. Avoid treating an SLO as a model-quality guarantee when its metric measures only infrastructure health.

topics.title: Resource monitoring
topics.description: Resource monitoring relates accelerator use, storage, and pipeline time to model value.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Resource monitoring relates accelerator use, storage, and pipeline time to model value. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Attribute resource cost
lessons.body: Track accelerator time, storage growth, and pipeline duration by experiment, model, and workload owner so expensive runs can be traced to a purpose. Aggregate platform totals alone hide inefficient or abandoned jobs.

lessons.title: Optimize against value and limits
lessons.body: Compare cost per useful prediction or validated model improvement with latency and quality constraints. Right-size hardware, schedule nonurgent jobs off peak, or stop redundant runs only after checking that the change preserves reproducibility and service objectives.

topics.title: A/B testing
topics.description: Randomized exposure compares model versions with guardrails and adequate sample size.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Randomized exposure compares model versions with guardrails and adequate sample size. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Design a valid comparison
lessons.body: Randomly assign eligible requests or users to stable control and treatment groups and define the primary metric before looking at results. Prevent a user from switching groups across requests when that would contaminate the comparison.

lessons.title: Respect guardrails and uncertainty
lessons.body: Check sample size, duration, segment balance, and confidence intervals alongside quality and safety guardrails. Stop or roll back for a predeclared harm threshold; do not declare a winner from a short, repeatedly inspected experiment.

topics.title: Reproducible recovery
topics.description: Recovery restores artifacts and workflow state while avoiding partial or duplicate outputs.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Recovery restores artifacts and workflow state while avoiding partial or duplicate outputs. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Checkpoint coherent state
lessons.body: Persist immutable inputs, successful task outputs, configuration, and lineage at boundaries where a workflow can resume safely. Do not mark a partially written artifact as complete or rely on mutable 'latest' paths after a failure.

lessons.title: Make retries idempotent
lessons.body: A retry should either reuse a verified output for the same input identity or safely replace it atomically, without duplicating external side effects. After recovery, compare checksums and lineage to confirm the final artifact matches the intended run.

topics.title: Feature store architecture
topics.description: Feature stores coordinate offline and online access, freshness, ownership, and point-in-time correctness.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A feature store manages feature definitions and access for model workflows. Offline paths often support historical training data; online paths serve recent features for low-latency predictions. The architecture must specify ownership, materialization, access controls, and consistency rather than assuming a product automatically provides them.

lessons.title: Build point-in-time examples
lessons.body: For each historical prediction, join the entity to feature values available at that prediction time. Distinguish event time from the time a value became available, including publication delays and corrections. A value published after the decision can leak future information even if it describes an earlier event.

lessons.title: Set freshness contracts
lessons.body: Document the expected update cadence, acceptable staleness, and behavior when a feature is missing or late. A stale value may be acceptable for one feature but harmful for another. Monitor freshness and make fallback behavior explicit to the serving application.

lessons.title: Protect parity and lineage
lessons.body: Version feature definitions and record the sources, transformation, and data timestamps used for a model. Test equivalent offline and online transformations using the same inputs and point-in-time assumptions. Compare boundary cases such as missing categories and late-arriving records.

lessons.title: Operate with ownership
lessons.body: Assign owners for feature definitions, quality checks, access policy, and incident response. Review consumer impact before changing semantics or deleting a feature, and monitor usage and costs. Centralizing feature access does not eliminate the need for data quality and model evaluation.

topics.title: Continuous training governance
topics.description: Continuous training creates candidates automatically but retains validation, approval, and rollback boundaries.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Continuous training automates creation of new model candidates as data or code changes. Training a candidate is distinct from approving and deploying it; automation should preserve explicit quality and governance checks.

lessons.title: Validate inputs
lessons.body: Check source freshness, schema, data quality, and point-in-time correctness before training. Record the data snapshot and code versions. If a check fails, stop or route the run for investigation instead of silently training on invalid inputs.

lessons.title: Evaluate candidates
lessons.body: Compare the candidate with a relevant baseline using representative data, task metrics, and important subgroup checks where feasible. Inspect uncertainty and resource constraints. Automated thresholds should reflect the intended use and cannot cover every failure mode.

lessons.title: Gate promotion
lessons.body: Apply the required approval and deployment policy after evaluation. A candidate that passes automated checks is not necessarily authorized for production. Record the decision, artifact versions, and evidence needed to understand what was promoted.

lessons.title: Monitor and roll back
lessons.body: Observe production quality, operational metrics, and data changes after rollout. Keep a tested rollback path to a compatible previous model and preprocessing package. Retraining on recent data can introduce new failures, so monitor outcomes rather than assuming freshness ensures quality.

topics.title: Version compatibility
topics.description: Compatibility contracts prevent serving a model with mismatched feature or preprocessing versions.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: A model depends on the features and preprocessing used during training. Compatibility rules specify which model, feature definitions, and transformations can be served together.

lessons.title: Record the bundle
lessons.body: Record the model artifact, expected feature schema, preprocessing version, and relevant dependencies as a versioned release. Include feature names, types, units, and ordering when the model relies on them.

lessons.title: Check compatibility
lessons.body: Validate the serving inputs and preprocessing against the model's declared expectations before promotion. Matching names alone is insufficient if units, category mappings, or transformation semantics changed.

lessons.title: Test representative inputs
lessons.body: Run known examples through both training and serving paths and compare resulting features with appropriate tolerances. Include missing and boundary values. A passing schema check cannot detect every semantic mismatch.

lessons.title: Release and recover together
lessons.body: Promote compatible artifacts together and keep their identifiers in deployment records. Monitor feature and prediction behavior after rollout. A rollback must restore a compatible combination, not merely an older model file.

topics.title: Safe rollback
topics.description: Rollback accounts for schemas, consumers, and in-flight requests as well as model weights.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Rollback returns a service to a known compatible release after a problem. The release includes more than model weights: preprocessing, schemas, dependencies, and consumer expectations may also need to change.

lessons.title: Keep a compatible release
lessons.body: Record and retain the prior model, feature definitions, preprocessing, configuration, and relevant runtime artifacts. Verify that the combination remains deployable and permitted by retention policy.

lessons.title: Consider traffic and state
lessons.body: Plan how to route new requests and handle in-flight work during a rollback. Stateful or asynchronous operations may require extra coordination to avoid duplicate work or incompatible results. Define what clients observe during the transition.

lessons.title: Check dependencies
lessons.body: An older model may expect a feature or response schema that current producers and consumers no longer support. Test compatibility across those boundaries before relying on a rollback. A successful artifact download is not a compatibility test.

lessons.title: Practice and observe
lessons.body: Exercise rollback in a representative environment, document triggers and responsibilities, and monitor errors, latency, and model behavior afterward. Investigate the original incident before retrying the failed release.

topics.title: Fleet management
topics.description: Fleet management coordinates ownership, versions, resource contention, and risk across deployed models.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Model fleet management coordinates many deployed models rather than treating each deployment in isolation. It tracks ownership, versions, shared resources, and operational risk across the portfolio.

lessons.title: Maintain an inventory
lessons.body: Record each deployment's owner, purpose, model and preprocessing versions, dependencies, and environment. Identify who can respond when a service fails or an artifact needs review.

lessons.title: Manage shared capacity
lessons.body: Models can compete for accelerator memory, compute, or serving throughput. Monitor utilization and latency by workload, and define capacity and prioritization policies. A healthy aggregate can conceal an overloaded individual service.

lessons.title: Control changes
lessons.body: Coordinate rollouts, compatibility checks, and rollback readiness across affected services. Shared dependencies can create correlated failures, so record which models use them and avoid assuming every deployment is independent.

lessons.title: Review fleet risk
lessons.body: Track stale models, unmet ownership or evaluation requirements, incidents, and resource saturation. Use the inventory to prioritize review and retirement. Apply privacy and retention policies to the operational records.

topics.title: Federated operations
topics.description: Federated workflows coordinate clients and aggregation while managing privacy, availability, and non-IID data.

lessons.title: Coordinate a training round
lessons.body: In federated learning, a coordinator distributes a model or training instructions to participating clients, which compute local updates. The coordinator aggregates accepted updates into a new global model according to a defined rule. Raw training data need not be sent to the coordinator, but updates and metadata can still be sensitive. A round needs clear selection, deadlines, authentication, and model-version rules.

lessons.title: Manage availability and versions
lessons.body: Clients can be offline, slow, or running different software versions. Define participation and minimum-response requirements, round timeouts, and how to handle stale or incompatible updates. If too few valid updates arrive, abort or defer according to the policy rather than silently treating the round as representative. Record which model version and configuration each accepted update used.

lessons.title: Account for non-IID data
lessons.body: Client datasets may differ in label prevalence, feature distributions, and size. An aggregate improvement can conceal poor performance for some client populations, and a client-weighting rule changes whose data has the greatest influence. Compare relevant client or population slices where privacy and sample sizes allow. Interpret small-sample results cautiously and consider participation bias when clients join unevenly.

lessons.title: Choose privacy protections
lessons.body: Keeping raw records on clients is not by itself a privacy guarantee: model updates can reveal information. Secure aggregation and differential privacy address different risks and require explicit threat models and correct implementation. Differential privacy also needs a defined privacy accounting mechanism and an assessed utility trade-off. Control metadata access and comply with the applicable data-handling rules.

lessons.title: Monitor the deployed process
lessons.body: Track participation, timeout rates, update acceptance, model versions, and aggregate quality over time. Investigate whether a drop in participation changes which populations influence training. Test rollback and recovery with compatible model and coordinator versions, and document why a round was accepted or rejected. Limit telemetry to what operators need and protect it as potentially sensitive.

topics.title: Pipeline privacy
topics.description: Privacy controls cover collection, transformation, access, logging, backups, and derived artifacts.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Privacy controls cover collection, transformation, access, logging, backups, and derived artifacts. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Map data across the lifecycle
lessons.body: Inventory sensitive fields as they move through ingestion, feature transforms, training snapshots, logs, caches, backups, and derived artifacts. Removing a field from the source table is insufficient if a copy remains in an export or retained model input record.

lessons.title: Enforce verifiable controls
lessons.body: Apply purpose-limited collection, role-based access, encryption, retention and deletion rules to each data store, and test that derived artifacts follow the applicable policy. Document exceptions and evidence without exposing the sensitive values themselves.

topics.title: Supply-chain security
topics.description: Supply-chain controls verify code, dependencies, datasets, and artifacts from source to deployment.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Supply-chain controls verify code, dependencies, datasets, and artifacts from source to deployment. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Establish artifact provenance
lessons.body: Bind a release artifact to reviewed source, pinned dependencies, build identity, dataset and configuration references, and a verifiable digest. A registry label alone does not establish that the artifact was built from trusted inputs.

lessons.title: Verify before deployment
lessons.body: Enforce signature or attestation checks and vulnerability policy at promotion time, then preserve the verification record with the deployed version. A failed or unverifiable dependency should block promotion until assessed and resolved under an explicit exception process.

topics.title: High-availability serving
topics.description: Availability requires redundancy, health-aware routing, capacity reserves, and tested failover.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Availability requires redundancy, health-aware routing, capacity reserves, and tested failover. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Design independent failure domains
lessons.body: Place redundant serving capacity across failure domains and route requests based on health, while ensuring each replica has compatible model and feature versions. Replicas sharing a single dependency or control plane do not provide full availability.

lessons.title: Prove failover under load
lessons.body: Reserve capacity for the loss of a zone and exercise failover with realistic traffic, dependency faults, and latency measurements. Validate recovery time and error budgets before claiming the design meets its availability target.

topics.title: Disaster recovery
topics.description: Recovery objectives cover artifacts, metadata, workflows, and serving state.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Recovery objectives cover artifacts, metadata, workflows, and serving state. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Set recovery objectives
lessons.body: Define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives for model artifacts, registry metadata, feature definitions, workflow state, and serving configuration. A backup strategy is incomplete if restoring model weights loses the provenance required to know how to serve them.

lessons.title: Test an end-to-end restore
lessons.body: Restore into an isolated environment, verify checksums and lineage, replay a representative workflow, and exercise compatible serving. Measure actual recovery against objectives and close gaps before relying on the backup plan.

topics.title: Drift diagnosis
topics.description: Diagnosis separates input drift, label shift, and concept change using data and outcome evidence.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Diagnosis separates input drift, label shift, and concept change using data and outcome evidence. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Separate competing hypotheses
lessons.body: Input drift changes feature distributions; label shift changes outcome prevalence; concept change alters the relationship between features and outcomes. Examine collection pipelines, cohort composition, and trustworthy labels to distinguish these causes.

lessons.title: Quantify impact before intervention
lessons.body: Estimate quality and decision impact by segment with uncertainty and compare against a stable reference. Select a targeted data fix, calibration, retraining, or rollback only when the evidence supports it and evaluation covers the affected population.

topics.title: Fairness monitoring
topics.description: Fairness monitoring tracks subgroup quality and coverage while accounting for privacy and population change.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Fairness monitoring tracks subgroup quality and coverage while accounting for privacy and population change. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Define meaningful subgroup measures
lessons.body: Select outcome and coverage metrics that reflect the model's intended decision and examine intersections where sample sizes support interpretation. Report denominators and uncertainty so a small or changing subgroup is not mistaken for stable evidence.

lessons.title: Govern privacy-aware response
lessons.body: Limit sensitive attribute access, document lawful measurement and retention, and avoid inferring protected traits from proxies without justification. Investigate confirmed disparities with domain owners and evaluate any mitigation for both subgroup effects and overall utility before rollout.

topics.title: Governance trails
topics.description: Governance requires attributable decisions, access history, approvals, and production-version evidence.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Governance requires attributable decisions, access history, approvals, and production-version evidence. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Record decision provenance
lessons.body: An audit trail links deployed version and data lineage to evaluations, policy checks, approvals, and the accountable decision-maker. Timestamps and immutable event records help reconstruct who authorized a release and on what evidence.

lessons.title: Make evidence reconstructable
lessons.body: Test whether an independent reviewer can retrieve the exact report, model digest, and approval chain for a historical deployment. Apply retention and access controls so evidence remains complete without retaining unnecessary sensitive payloads.

topics.title: Decommissioning
topics.description: Decommissioning removes traffic and credentials safely while preserving required records and deleting expired data.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Decommissioning removes traffic and credentials safely while preserving required records and deleting expired data. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Plan a controlled shutdown
lessons.body: Identify consumers, scheduled jobs, aliases, credentials, feature dependencies, and retention obligations before removing a model. Notify owners and route traffic elsewhere only after replacement behavior and rollback windows are understood.

lessons.title: Verify removal and retention
lessons.body: Drain traffic, revoke runtime credentials, remove obsolete resources, and verify that caches and derived data follow approved deletion schedules. Preserve required audit records and confirm no hidden client continues to call the retired endpoint.

topics.title: Platform scheduling
topics.description: Shared platforms need quotas and priority policies to prevent workload resource starvation.

lessons.title: Concept and application
lessons.body: Shared platforms need quotas and priority policies to prevent workload resource starvation. Apply this idea using representative examples, and verify its limits with an evaluation that matches the intended use.

lessons.title: Model shared workload demand
lessons.body: Estimate resource requests and deadlines across interactive inference, urgent retraining, and deferrable batch work. Quotas, priorities, and admission controls should reflect service criticality without allowing one team to reserve idle capacity indefinitely.

lessons.title: Protect fairness and reliability
lessons.body: Monitor queue delay, starvation, preemption, and accelerator utilization by tenant, then revise scheduling policy against explicit service targets. Test overload behavior and protect reserved serving capacity before accepting additional training workloads.
